levels.title: Philosophy in One Level
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what philosophy is, name its biggest questions and say how philosophers try to answer them with careful argument.

levels.title: The Branches of Philosophy
levels.objective: After this level you can name the main branches of philosophy (metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, logic, aesthetics and political philosophy) and the question each one asks.

levels.title: Thought Experiments
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how a thought experiment tests an idea by imagining a carefully built case instead of running a real one.

levels.title: Plato's World of Forms
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Plato's theory that perfect, unchanging Forms, like Circle or Justice, are more real than the things we see.

levels.title: Aristotle's Four Causes
levels.objective: After this level you can use Aristotle's four causes (material, formal, efficient and final) to explain what a bronze statue is and why it exists.

levels.title: Confucius and the Good Person
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Confucius's ideal of the junzi, the exemplary person, and his ideas of ren (humaneness) and li (ritual propriety).

levels.title: Laozi and the Way
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Dao of Laozi and Zhuangzi and the idea of wu wei, acting without forcing, using their image of water.

levels.title: The Buddha's Case Against a Self
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Buddhist no-self argument, using the monk Nagasena's chariot that is nothing over and above its parts.

levels.title: India's Schools of Philosophy
levels.objective: After this level you can name several classical Indian schools, including Nyaya, Vedanta, the materialist Carvaka and the Jains, and one idea each is known for.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Where Philosophy Began
levels.objective: After this level you can compare how Greek, Chinese and Indian thinkers first asked what is real and how to live.

levels.title: Avicenna's Floating Man
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Avicenna's floating man, a person created in midair with no sensations, and what it was meant to show about self-awareness.

levels.title: Al-Ghazali Versus Ibn Rushd
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the debate between al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers and Ibn Rushd's reply, including their dispute over fire burning cotton.

levels.title: Maimonides and the Perplexed
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Maimonides's Guide for the Perplexed tried to reconcile the Hebrew Bible with Aristotle, and his idea of describing God only by what God is not.

levels.title: Thomas Aquinas: Faith and Reason
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Thomas Aquinas combined Aristotle with Christian theology and why he held that faith and reason cannot truly conflict.

levels.title: Wang Yangming: Knowing Is Doing
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Wang Yangming's claim that knowledge and action are one, and the bamboo he stared at for days trying to find its principle.

levels.title: Descartes Doubts Everything
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Descartes's method of doubt, his dream and evil demon arguments, and why "I think, therefore I am" survived them.

levels.title: Spinoza and Leibniz
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what made Spinoza and Leibniz rationalists, with Spinoza's "God or Nature" and Leibniz's claim that this is the best possible world.

levels.title: Locke, Berkeley and Hume
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the empiricist claim that all ideas come from experience, from Locke's blank slate to Berkeley and Hume.

levels.title: Kant's Revolution
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Kant's claim that the mind shapes experience through space, time and cause, and how it answered both rationalists and empiricists.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Avicenna to Kant
levels.objective: After this level you can trace how medieval and early modern philosophers argued over reason, faith and experience from Avicenna to Kant.

levels.title: What Is Knowledge?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the classic definition of knowledge as justified true belief and what each of its three parts adds.

levels.title: The Gettier Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Edmund Gettier's 1963 cases, like the job applicant with ten coins in his pocket, show a lucky true belief falling short of knowledge.

levels.title: The Ancient Skeptics
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how Pyrrho and Sextus Empiricus balanced opposing arguments and suspended judgment in search of peace of mind.

levels.title: Brain in a Vat
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the brain-in-a-vat puzzle and how Hilary Putnam argued that you cannot coherently think you are one.

levels.title: Knowing Without Looking
levels.objective: After this level you can tell a priori knowledge, known by reason alone, from a posteriori knowledge, known through experience.

levels.title: Why Expect the Sun to Rise?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Hume's problem of induction: why any argument that the future will resemble the past seems to assume what it needs to prove.

levels.title: Nyaya's Sources of Knowledge
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Nyaya school's four sources of knowledge, including its classic inference from smoke on a hill to fire.

levels.title: What Makes a Belief True?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the correspondence theory of truth, matching the world, with the coherence theory, fitting with other beliefs.

levels.title: Truth That Works
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how the American pragmatists Peirce, James and Dewey tied truth and meaning to practical consequences.

levels.title: Checkpoint: What Can We Know?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain how philosophers define knowledge, where they think it comes from and how they answer the skeptic.

levels.title: The Mind-Body Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the mind-body problem: how thoughts and feelings relate to the physical brain and body.

levels.title: The Ghost in the Machine
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Descartes's dualism of mind and matter, Princess Elisabeth's question about how they interact, and Ryle's nickname for it.

levels.title: The Mind Is the Brain
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the identity theory, the physicalist view that each mental state simply is a brain state.

levels.title: Minds as Software
levels.objective: After this level you can explain functionalism, which defines mental states by what they do, and why it allows minds made of something other than neurons.

levels.title: Can Machines Think?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Alan Turing's 1950 imitation game and what passing it would and would not show.

levels.title: The Chinese Room
levels.objective: After this level you can explain John Searle's Chinese room and his argument that following rules for symbols is not the same as understanding.

levels.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Thomas Nagel's argument that science's outside view may leave out what an experience is like from the inside.

levels.title: Mary's Room
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Frank Jackson's Mary, who knows every physical fact about color, and the debate over whether she learns something new on seeing red.

levels.title: The Hard Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain David Chalmers's hard problem of consciousness and how it differs from the easy problems of explaining brain functions.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Mind and Consciousness
levels.objective: After this level you can compare dualism, physicalism and functionalism and say which puzzle about consciousness each struggles with.

levels.title: Is Morality Just Culture?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain moral relativism, using Herodotus's story of two peoples' opposite funeral customs, and the main objection to it.

levels.title: The Euthyphro Dilemma
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Plato's Euthyphro dilemma: is something good because God commands it, or commanded because it is good?

levels.title: The Ring of Gyges
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Glaucon asks whether anyone would stay just while wearing a ring of invisibility, and what the challenge asks of ethics.

levels.title: Is Human Nature Good?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare Mencius's view that people are born with the sprouts of goodness with Xunzi's view that goodness must be learned.

levels.title: Aristotle's Golden Mean
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Aristotle's virtue ethics, where courage sits between cowardice and recklessness and virtue is built by practice.

levels.title: The Greatest Happiness
levels.objective: After this level you can explain utilitarianism as Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill set it out, including Mill's higher and lower pleasures.

levels.title: Kant's Categorical Imperative
levels.objective: After this level you can apply Kant's categorical imperative, in its universal-law and never-merely-as-a-means forms, to a false promise.

levels.title: The Ethics of Care
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan and Nel Noddings and why it starts from relationships rather than rules.

levels.title: Hume's Is and Ought
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Hume's point that no conclusion about what ought to be follows from facts about what is alone.

levels.title: Milestone: Knowledge, Mind and Morals
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the first half's traditions, theories of knowledge, views of the mind and moral theories into one map of philosophy's big questions.

levels.title: Plato's Just City
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Plato's Republic argues for rule by philosopher-kings and how his three-class city mirrors a just soul.

levels.title: Virtue or Law?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why ancient China's Confucians trusted virtuous rulers while Legalists like Han Feizi trusted strict laws and punishments, and why each side thought so.

levels.title: Machiavelli's Prince
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Machiavelli advised rulers that it can be safer to be feared than loved, and why his name became an insult.

levels.title: Mill's Harm Principle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why John Stuart Mill argued that society may limit your liberty only to prevent harm to others.

levels.title: Wollstonecraft's Rights of Woman
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Mary Wollstonecraft argued in 1792 that women seem less rational only because they are denied education.

levels.title: Marx on Work and Class
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Karl Marx thought workers under capitalism were alienated, and the main objections critics raised.

levels.title: Beauvoir's Second Sex
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Simone de Beauvoir wrote that "one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman" and what she meant by woman as the Other.

levels.title: Rawls's Veil of Ignorance
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why John Rawls asks you to choose society's rules without knowing your place in it, and the principles he thought you would pick.

levels.title: Nozick and Wilt Chamberlain
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why Robert Nozick used a basketball star's ticket sales to argue that liberty upsets any fixed pattern of fair shares.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Justice and the Good Society
levels.objective: After this level you can compare the reasons thinkers give for who should rule, how free people should be and what makes a society just.

levels.title: Is Everything Already Caused?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain determinism, using Laplace's all-knowing intellect, and why it seems to threaten free will.

levels.title: The Case for Free Choice
levels.objective: After this level you can explain libertarian free will, the view that some choices are not fixed by prior causes, and why its defenders find it necessary for blame and praise.

levels.title: Free Because You Want It
levels.objective: After this level you can explain compatibilism, the view of Hobbes and Hume that freedom means acting on your own wants, not escaping causes, using Hobbes's water flowing down its channel.

levels.title: Frankfurt's Hidden Controller
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Harry Frankfurt's 1969 case of a controller who never has to act, and why it suggests responsibility doesn't need the power to do otherwise.

levels.title: Condemned to Be Free
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence and his idea of bad faith, using his café waiter who plays at being a waiter.

levels.title: Locke's Prince and Cobbler
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Locke's memory theory of personal identity, using a prince's memories waking up in a cobbler's body.

levels.title: The Ship of Theseus
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Ship of Theseus puzzle and why rebuilding the ship from its old planks makes the question harder.

levels.title: The Teleporter Puzzle
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Derek Parfit's teleporter and fission cases and his conclusion that identity may matter less than we think.

levels.title: A Person Through Other People
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the southern African idea of ubuntu, that a person is a person through other persons, and how it challenges a purely individual self.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Freedom and the Self
levels.objective: After this level you can connect the debates over free will and personal identity to earlier views of the mind and the self.

levels.title: Plato's Cave, Revisited
levels.objective: After this level you can explain what Plato's cave argues about appearance, reality and education, and why Aristotle and the empiricists rejected its two worlds.

levels.title: Zeno's Impossible Race
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise and how the mathematics of infinite series is often said to answer it.

levels.title: Augustine and the Puzzle of Time
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Augustine's puzzle that the past is gone, the future not yet here and the present has no length, and his answer in the mind.

levels.title: Why Is There Something?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Leibniz's question of why there is something rather than nothing and his answer from sufficient reason.

levels.title: The Ontological Argument
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Anselm's ontological argument for God, Gaunilo's perfect island reply and Kant's objection that existence is not a property.

levels.title: The First Cause
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the cosmological argument in al-Ghazali's and Aquinas's versions and the objection "what caused the first cause?".

levels.title: The Watchmaker Argument
levels.objective: After this level you can explain William Paley's argument from a watch found on a heath and the replies from Hume and from Darwin's theory of evolution.

levels.title: The Problem of Evil
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the problem of evil as philosophers state it and the free will reply offered by Augustine and, later, Alvin Plantinga.

levels.title: When Words Make Puzzles
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the later Wittgenstein's idea that meaning is use and why he thought some philosophical puzzles come from language misfiring.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Reality, Time and God
levels.objective: After this level you can connect puzzles about reality, time and God's existence to the earlier chapters' tools of reason and experience.

levels.title: The Trolley Problem
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Philippa Foot's trolley problem and use it to test whether saving five by diverting harm to one is allowed.

levels.title: The Footbridge
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why many people who would pull the switch refuse to push a man off a footbridge, and how the doctrine of double effect tries to explain the difference.

levels.title: The Drowning Child
levels.objective: After this level you can apply Peter Singer's drowning child argument to the question of how much we owe distant strangers, and weigh the main replies.

levels.title: Can They Suffer?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh the arguments of Bentham, Singer and their critics about whether animals' suffering counts morally as much as ours.

levels.title: The Murderer at the Door
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh Kant's claim that you may not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding against a consequentialist reply.

levels.title: Moral Luck
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Bernard Williams's and Thomas Nagel's puzzle of moral luck, using two equally careless drivers with different outcomes.

levels.title: Family First or Everyone Equal?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh Mozi's impartial care for all against the Confucian view that love rightly starts with your own family.

levels.title: Do We Owe Future People?
levels.objective: After this level you can explain why duties to people not yet born are puzzling, including Parfit's non-identity problem, and apply it to a long-term choice.

levels.title: Could a Machine Matter Morally?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh what earlier theories of mind and morals imply about whether an artificial system could ever deserve moral concern.

levels.title: Checkpoint: Hard Moral Choices
levels.objective: After this level you can reason through a new moral dilemma with at least two moral theories and say where they agree and split.

levels.title: Is Beauty in the Eye of the Beholder?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh Hume's standard of taste against Kant's claim that a judgment of beauty speaks for everyone.

levels.title: What Makes Something Art?
levels.objective: After this level you can compare three answers to "what is art?" (imitation, expression and the institutional theory) and apply them to an unusual case.

levels.title: Epicurus on Fearing Death
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Epicurus's argument that death is nothing to us, and weigh the reply that death harms us by taking away future goods.

levels.title: The Stoic Split
levels.objective: After this level you can explain the Stoic line between what is up to us and what is not, as Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius taught it, and apply it to a setback.

levels.title: The Experience Machine
levels.objective: After this level you can use Robert Nozick's experience machine to weigh whether pleasure is all that makes a life go well.

levels.title: Nietzsche's Eternal Return
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Nietzsche's test of living your life again forever and why he thought saying yes to it mattered after "God is dead".

levels.title: Camus and the Absurd
levels.objective: After this level you can explain Camus's absurd, the clash between our demand for meaning and a silent world, and why he pictured Sisyphus happy.

levels.title: What Makes a Life Meaningful?
levels.objective: After this level you can weigh views of meaning in life that locate it in God's purpose, in what you care about, or in Susan Wolf's mix of caring and real worth.

levels.title: Thinking Like a Philosopher
levels.objective: After this level you can take a new big question through the tree's toolkit: clarify the terms, test it with a thought experiment, and weigh the rival views.

levels.title: Mastery Challenge: Philosophy
levels.objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Philosophy Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
